terms.definition: Secure Shell — a cryptographic network protocol for secure remote login and command execution over an unsecured network.
terms.example: ssh -i mykey.pem ec2-user@54.123.45.67

terms.definition: The secret half of an SSH key pair, stored on your local machine. Used to authenticate your identity to a server. Never share this.
terms.example: ~/.ssh/id_rsa is the default location for your private key

terms.definition: The shareable half of an SSH key pair. Stored on the remote server in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The server uses it to verify your private key.
terms.example: ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub is the default public key file

terms.definition: A file on the server at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys that lists all public keys allowed to log in to that user account.
terms.example: Each line in authorized_keys holds one public key

terms.definition: A command-line tool used to generate a new SSH key pair (both private and public key).
terms.example: ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C your@email.com

terms.definition: A command that automatically copies your public key to a remote server's authorized_keys file.
terms.example: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub vikram@192.168.1.1

terms.definition: The SSH daemon configuration file at /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Controls server-side SSH behavior including whether password authentication is allowed.
terms.example: Set PasswordAuthentication yes in this file to allow password login

terms.definition: Rivest-Shamir-Adleman — a widely used asymmetric encryption algorithm used for generating SSH key pairs.
terms.example: ssh-keygen -t rsa generates an RSA key pair

terms.definition: Change mode — the Linux command used to change the read, write, and execute permissions on files and directories.
terms.example: chmod 755 script.sh gives owner full access and group/others read+execute

terms.definition: Change owner — the Linux command used to change who owns a file or directory.
terms.example: sudo chown vikram:devops myfile.txt changes owner to vikram and group to devops

terms.definition: Change group — the Linux command used to change only the group associated with a file.
terms.example: sudo chgrp developers /shared/project

terms.definition: User file creation mask — a value that controls the default permissions applied when new files and directories are created.
terms.example: A umask of 022 results in new files getting 644 and new directories getting 755

terms.definition: Set User ID — a special permission bit that makes an executable run with the file owner's permissions rather than the launching user's.
terms.example: The passwd command has SUID set so regular users can change their password

terms.definition: Set Group ID — a special permission bit on a directory that makes new files inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group.
terms.example: Set SGID on /shared/project so all files there belong to the 'devteam' group

terms.definition: A special permission on directories that prevents users from deleting files they don't own, even if they have write access to the directory.
terms.example: /tmp always has the sticky bit set (shown as 't' in ls -l output)

terms.definition: The three Linux permission types: r=read (view content), w=write (modify content), x=execute (run as program or traverse directory).
terms.example: drwxr-xr-x shows full permissions for owner, read+execute for group and others

terms.definition: The user account that created a file or directory. Shown as the 3rd column in ls -l output. Has the first set of rwx permissions.
terms.example: In '-rw-r--r-- 1 vikram devops file.txt', vikram is the owner

terms.definition: A named collection of users in Linux. The group assigned to a file determines which users get the group permission set.
terms.example: Adding developers to the 'devops' group lets them use group-level file access

terms.definition: All users on the system who are not the file's owner and not a member of the file's group. Gets the last 3 characters of the permission string.
terms.example: In chmod 755, the final '5' sets r-x permissions for others

terms.definition: A Windows application that provides a Bash terminal environment, allowing Windows users to run Linux commands including SSH tools.
terms.example: Install Git Bash from git-scm.com to use ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id on Windows

terms.definition: An AWS feature allowing browser-based SSH access to EC2 instances directly from the AWS console without a local SSH client.
terms.example: Click Connect → EC2 Instance Connect in the AWS console to access a server in-browser

terms.definition: A setting in /etc/ssh/sshd_config that controls whether password-based SSH login is permitted. Default is 'no' on Amazon Linux.
terms.example: Set PasswordAuthentication yes and restart sshd to enable password login
